A historic example is railroad regulation. When railroads were first regulated, prices skyrocketed and routes shrank. Airlines are another good example: up until de-regulation in the 80s, airlines (like trucking companies in the 60s) ran predefined government-imposed routes at utility fares. Libertarianism can be divided more or less into two camps. The ones you are referring to I've heard referred to as "big L Libertarians." These are the guys who believe in private fire departments, completely free markets, no interventions in foreign affairs, and that the government should only exist to defend its population. Credit where credit is due, these people are strong in their beliefs and have kept the philosophy alive and provided the core of the party.

The other group that is far more numerous are "small L libertarians." These are generally your younger Rand/Ron Paul fans who believe in the scaling back of government, but not the pursuit of a total anarcho-capitalism. Their objectives and beliefs can be summed up generally as...

  1. End US intervention in foreign affairs.

  2. Scale back the growth of the federal government. (Reduce redundant federal agencies such as intelligence agencies, federal agencies that duplicate state agencies such as Dept of Education/IRS)

  3. Restore all rights back to individuals that don't harm others. So, no murder, no arson, and interestingly a strong stance against polluting. This is the foundation for why many people who enjoy marijuana and firearms flock to the banner.

  4. Decrease government regulation to the point where small businesses can enter the market. Regulatory compliance rarely affects large corporations. Comcast and Walmart can afford to hire another hundred lawyers to ensure they comply with Dodd-Frank or international trade practices. Your local general store cannot pay a lawyer full time to ensure they're properly complying when their profit margin is 1 or 2%.

In summary, you've been reading or talking to Libertarians, not libertarians. It's kind of akin to talking to Karl Marx instead of Bernie Sanders. Or talking to Ayn Rand instead of Eisenhower. When you take the purist view of Libertarianism, it's pretty wild. When you accept that it's okay to hold complicated views with qualifiers and caveats, then it makes much more sense. "Who's killing the hydrogen car?" A bunch of facts that don't make it viable at the moment, I'd figure.

http://grist.org/business-technology/why-arent-we-all-driving-hydrogen-fuel-cell-cars/
Yeah, electrolysis is horribly inefficient. You do it in science class because it's a simple demonstration, not because it's a practical way to obtain hydrogen for fuel purposes.

This is irrelevant since it would be possible for every individual to setup a solar panel and run the electrolysis for free. It would probably be inconvenient due to the amount of time it would take to fill the tank however. But we can get the power needed for electrolysis from solar or wind power instead of burning fossil fuels.

The only cost is the water if you are on public water. The initial cost would be higher than fossil fuel cars due to having to buy specialized equipment, but the savings would be realized in the cost of fuel. Plus it is much better for the environment since it produces oxygen in the creation of the fuel and water after combustion.

I'm not a chemist or physicist, but why would you capture solar energy and then use that to create hydrogen and then create electricity to power the mechanical bits when you could just go straight from solar to electricity to mechanical power? I don't see where the hydrogen is needed in that step, given the state of electric cars today.

I am also not a scientist, but I believe the main issue is storage of energy. Batteries are expensive and solar is slow. So by using that energy to create hydride we can safely store this in a gas tank. It can then be released into the chamber to be combusted to provide energy.

Its efficiency is extremely relevant. There are a myriad of variables you're ignoring. For one thing, pure H2O does not conduct electricity. You have to introduce impurities, specifically an electrolyte. The type of electrolyte you use even has an effect on whether any hydrogen gas is produced at all. Variance in water supplies means that not only is this process inefficient to begin with, but you're going to have varying levels of efficiency depending upon what electrolytes are already present in your water. Once you've created the gas, you now have to capture and compress it into a storage tank. This also requires energy.

Battery technology is moving forward rapidly. Tesla has already decided to double the capacity of its in-home power pack while keeping the price the same. There are many consumer industries using batteries who will benefit a great deal from any advances. There is a lot of R&D happening in this arena around the world because the market is demanding it. Most of the world already has an electrical grid. We already have a well maintained means of transporting energy around the world. Why would we expend energy capturing and transporting hydrogen when we could just move the energy directly? Ethanol has this same problem - you use more energy producing it and transporting it than you get from actually burning it. It's a negative equation, it makes no sense.

While you are not wrong, I don't see the downside of pursuing both technologies. Why not give the consumer many options? What about when we run out of natural resources required to make batteries? Focusing solely on a single technology is what got us into this position with fossil fuels to begin with.

I also disagree with your assertion at the inefficiency of hydrogen cell cars.

http://auto.howstuffworks.com/fuel-efficiency/fuel-saving-devices/energy-efficiency-ratio-hydrogen-fuel-cell1.htm

*Edit - TL;DR of that link. Efficiency is 60-85% while normal cars get around 60% efficiency.

You skipped too much reading, it said the sort of fuel cell used in a car is only 50-60% efficient. ;)

At any rate, I'm not saying that hydrogen is an inherently terrible fuel. I'm saying acquiring it, storing, and transporting it are what make it inefficient. If we could easily get it then that may offset the additional cost and wasted energy of transporting it and storing it.

I'm all for competition. My point from the start was - no one is killing the hydrogen car, it's DOA for a myriad of reasons including the fact that the most plentiful source of it that we have (H2O) happens to really like its hydrogen atom, and getting it to let it go is expensive. Whoa man, that looks creepy as hell!

I think the lesson here is nature will always find a way.

If humans disappeared from the planet tomorrow, it wouldn't take long for even the most densely urbanised places to be completely overrun by nature.

And that's the opportunity that the nature organizations missed out on in the 80s when they started campaigning for green alternatives. They shouldn't have gone "here, look at this sad panda, if you take your car to work, one day he won't live. Don't you feel guilty?" What they should have said was "here, look at this epic disaster, look how nature takes everything back. See the lack of humans in this picture? Yes, this is what's going to happen to the entire planet one day."

I'm not afraid for the environment one bit. We can pretty much nuke the shit out of everything, throw every kind of carcinogen out there everywhere, turn the water into oil, turn the forests into kindling, saturate the atmosphere with carbon until we all choke. Lifes response to that? Alright, challenge accepted. I'll just evolve radiation resistance.. hell, I'll even make myself thrive of it. Carcinogens? You mean faster mutation rates? I'm down with that says evolution. Oil instead of water? Alrighty, I'll just get some bacteria to eat it instead! No oxygen? No problem, who needs breathing anyway?
If environmental organizations took that approach it would garner less support.
